note: These are published major defects and varieties, not a line for every date. Specialist catalogs such as CONECA, Wexler, and the VAM list add many minor ones. Off-center strikes, clips, cuds, and wrong planchets can happen in any year and are not repeated under each date.

1909: 1909 VDB and 1909 no VDB are two types. A doubled die obverse on the VDB cent is a known variety. Look at the initials and LIBERTY.
1917: 1917 doubled die obverse. Check LIBERTY and the date.
1922: 1922 No D, or plain, from a worn Denver die. The mint mark is missing or very weak and the reverse is sharp on the strong variety.
1936: 1936 doubled die obverse is a known Lincoln variety. The spread is smaller than 1955.
1943: Normal 1943 cents are steel and stick to a magnet. A bronze 1943 cent is a wrong-planchet rarity. Steel 1943 doubled dies and repunched mint marks are also listed.
1944: A steel 1944 cent is a wrong-planchet rarity and sticks to a magnet. 1944-D/S is a listed overmintmark.
1955: 1955 doubled die obverse, Philadelphia. The date, LIBERTY, and IN GOD WE TRUST show a wide second image. A 1955 with only flat machine doubling is the so-called poor man's doubled die and is not that coin.
1958: 1958 doubled die obverse is a major rarity, not a coin you should expect in change.

1959: Doubled dies are reported. Most are minor.
1960: 1960 and 1960-D large date and small date. Compare the 6 and the 0.
1969: 1969-S doubled die obverse. LIBERTY and the date are strongly doubled. The S mint mark is not doubled.
1970: 1970-S large date and small date. Doubled dies are also reported.
1972: 1972 doubled die obverse. Several dies. The strong one shows a clear spread on IN GOD WE TRUST and LIBERTY.
1982: Large date and small date, and both copper and zinc planchets. A 1982-D small-date cent that weighs about 3.11 grams is the scarce copper transitional.
1983: 1983 doubled die reverse. UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, ONE CENT, and E PLURIBUS UNUM show the spread. A copper 1983-D is a reported transitional.
1984: 1984 doubled ear. A second lobe sits under Lincoln's ear.
1988: 1988 no FG, the designer's initials missing on the reverse, is listed as a variety.
1990: 1990 no-S proof cent. Proofs only. The S is missing.
1992: 1992 and 1992-D close AM. The A and M in AMERICA are close together, the proof style, on a business strike.
1995: 1995 doubled die obverse. Look for a spread on LIBERTY, especially the last letters.
1998: 1998, 1999, and 2000 wide AM. The letters A and M in AMERICA sit farther apart. 1999 is the scarce one.
1999: 1999 wide AM. A and M in AMERICA are widely spaced. This is the key date of the wide AM group.
2000: 2000 wide AM. Same AM test as 1998 and 1999. Less scarce than 1999.

2019: A doubled die reverse is reported. The spread is usually small and needs a loupe.
2021: A doubled die reverse is reported. Check the shield lettering under a loupe.
2022: A doubled die reverse is reported. Most examples are minor.

1913: 1913 Type 1 has the buffalo on a raised mound. Type 2 has a straight line under the buffalo.
1916: 1916 doubled die obverse is a known variety. Check the date and the feathers.
1918: 1918/7-D is an overdate on the Denver nickel. Look at the 7 under the 8.
1936: 1936 doubled die obverse is a listed Buffalo variety.
1937: 1937-D three-legged. The front leg is missing because the die was overpolished. Check the reverse, not the date.

1939: 1939 reverses exist from the 1938 hub and the 1940 hub. The steps and lettering differ.
1942: Some 1942 nickels are the regular alloy. Later 1942 coins with a large P, D, or S over the dome are 35 percent silver.
1943: 1943, 1944, and 1945 with the large mint mark over the dome are silver war nickels. 1943-P doubled eye is a listed variety. Look at Jefferson's eye.
1944: Silver war nickel if the large mint mark sits over the dome.
1945: Silver war nickel if the large mint mark sits over the dome.

2004: Two reverses: Peace Medal and Keelboat. A doubled die is not the thing to hunt. Confirm which reverse you have.
2005: 2005-D speared bison and 2005-D detached leg are the listed defects. Look at the bison's legs and belly.

1941: 1941-D doubled die obverse and reverse are listed.
1942: 1942/1 and 1942/1-D overdates. Look at the 2 in the date. A 1 shows under it.
1945: 1945 doubled die obverse is listed. 1945-S micro S is a small mint mark.

1964: 1964-D doubled die is a listed dime variety. Also the last 90 percent silver year.
1965: A 1965 dime struck on a silver planchet is a transitional error. Normal 1965 dimes are clad.
1975: 1975 no-S proof. Proofs only. Very rare.
1982: 1982 no P. A Philadelphia business strike missing the P mint mark.

1916: 1916 is the rare first year. It is a date rarity, not a die defect.
1917: 1917 Type 1 has no chain mail. Type 2 covers Liberty's chest with chain mail.
1918: 1918/7-S is the famous overdate. Look at the date.

1932: 1932-D and 1932-S are scarce dates, not die defects.
1934: 1934 light, medium, and heavy motto. The motto IN GOD WE TRUST was strengthened during the year.
1937: 1937 doubled die obverse is a listed quarter variety.
1942: 1942-D doubled die obverse is a listed variety.
1943: 1943-S doubled die obverse, often called the goiter variety, shows extra metal on Washington's neck.
1952: 1952 superbird. The eagle's wing tip was re-engraved.

1999: State quarters of many years have minor doubled dies. 1999 is not one of the famous extra-leaf coins.
2004: 2004-D Wisconsin extra leaf. A high leaf or a low leaf sticks up from the ear of corn. Philadelphia coins are the normal design.
2005: 2005 Minnesota doubled dies and extra-tree dies are the listed state-quarter defects. Look at the trees by the lake.

1964: 1964 accented hair, mostly on proofs: stronger hair above the ear and a weak serif on the I in LIBERTY. 1964 and 1964-D doubled dies show spread on IN GOD WE TRUST. 1964 is also 90 percent silver.
1966: 1966 SMS doubled die obverse is a listed variety. Some special-strike coins are missing the FG initials.
1971: A 1971-D struck on a silver planchet is a transitional error. Normal 1971 halves are clad.
1972: 1972-D no FG. The designer's initials are missing from the reverse because the die was polished too hard.
1974: 1974-D doubled die obverse. Strong spread on IN GOD WE TRUST and LIBERTY. This is the major clad doubled die of the series.
1976: 1776-1976 clad halves spend near face. 1976-S silver is a collector issue, not a defect.
1977: A 1977-D on a silver planchet is a reported transitional.
1982: 1982-P no FG. Missing designer initials on the reverse.

1917: 1917-D and 1917-S come with the mint mark on the obverse or the reverse. Obverse mint marks are the scarcer pair.
1946: 1946 doubled die reverse is a listed Walking Liberty variety.

1878: 1878 comes with 8 tail feathers, 7 tail feathers, and 7 over 8 tail feathers. Count the feathers and look for a second set underneath.
1880: 1880/79 overdates are listed on some Carson City and Philadelphia dies.
1882: 1882-O/S is an overmintmark. Look at the mint mark.
1888: 1888-O hot lips. Doubling on Liberty's lips and nose from a doubled die.
1900: 1900-O/CC. An O mint mark punched over a CC. Look inside the O.
1901: 1901 doubled die reverse is a listed Morgan variety.

1921: 1921 is high relief. The cheek and eagle often look weak. That is the design, not damage, when the rim lettering is sharp.
1922: 1922 onwards is the lower relief. A 1922 high-relief strike is a rarity, not the normal coin.
1934: 1934-D doubled die obverse is a listed Peace dollar variety.

1979: 1979-P near date, also called wide rim. The date sits closer to the rim than on the far-date coins.
1981: 1981-S proof comes with a filled S and a clear S.

2000: 2000-P Cheerios dollar. The prototype reverse has extra detail in the eagle's tail feathers. It came in Cheerios boxes, not in ordinary change.

1971: 1971-S and some later S mint silver collector strikes are 40 percent silver. A clad Ike from change is the normal coin.
1972: 1972 has three reverse varieties. Type 2 has the Earth more rounded between the islands. Type 3 is the later, sharper reverse.
1976: 1776-1976 clad and 1776-1976 silver collector strikes. Silver ones were sold in Mint packaging.

1859: 1859 has a laurel wreath reverse. 1860 changed to an oak wreath and shield.
1864: 1864 comes in copper-nickel and in thinner bronze. Bronze coins with the L on the ribbon are a variety.
1888: 1888 over 7 is a reported overdate. It is scarce.

1883: 1883 without CENTS and 1883 with CENTS. The no-CENTS coin is a type, and many were gold-plated later. Plating is damage, not a mint defect.
1913: 1913 Liberty nickel is a famous rarity with only a handful known. A normal 1912 or 1913 Buffalo is not this coin.

1866: 1866 and early 1867 have rays on the reverse. Later 1867 and after have no rays.

1853: 1853 arrows at the date, and some with arrows and rays, mark a weight change. Arrows are the design, not damage.
1873: 1873 arrows at the date, and closed or open 3 varieties.

1853: 1853 arrows and rays, then arrows without rays. The arrows are a weight-change design.

1955: 1955 bugs bunny. A die clash makes Franklin look like he has buck teeth. Look at the mouth.

1892: 1892-O micro O is a small mint mark variety.

1875: Chop marks are later commercial stamps, not a mint defect. Note them and do not call them cuds.
